This article is an open access article distributed under the terms and conditions of the <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/" ext-link-type="uri">Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) license</ext-link>.</license-p></license></permissions><self-uri xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="biology-15-01782.pdf" content-type="pmc-pdf"><?cloudpmc-path 78de/13664187/3e5e8d9efe8f/biology-15-01782.pdf?><?cloudpmc-bucket app?><?size 10427456?></self-uri><abstract id="abstract1" abstract-type="plain-language-summary"><title>Simple Summary</title><p>Identifying genes cancer cells need to survive or grow may help researchers choose experimental targets. Direct testing is difficult and costly in organoids, which are small three-dimensional models grown from patient tumors. Using gene activity measurements from 852 conventional cancer models, we built predictive models for a preselected panel of 20 genes. Our primary evaluation asked whether the models could rank organoids by their dependence on each gene. Performance was weaker in organoids, but a small signal remained in 94 Broad organoids and in 148 Sanger organoids from 144 donors. Predictions for the Sanger organoids were fixed before the measured outcomes were accessed. A separate retrospective analysis examined whether the same predictions could rank the 20 genes within each organoid. This retrospective analysis showed modest improvement over tumor-lineage predictions for the full ranking, while improvement for the three strongest measured dependencies was observed only in Sanger. Pancreatic organoid results remained projections because direct measurements were unavailable. These findings provide limited evidence for ranking genes within the selected panel. They do not establish which experiments will succeed or which treatments will work in patients.</p><sec id="kwd-group1" sec-type="kwd-group" disp-level="2"><p><bold>Keywords:</bold> gene dependency, patient-derived organoids, functional genomics, transcriptomics, CRISPR screening, Elastic Net, external validation, cross-model transferability</p></sec></abstract><abstract id="abstract2"><title>Abstract</title><p>Transferability of transcriptome-based gene-dependency models from two-dimensional cancer models to organoids remains uncertain. Expression-only Elastic Net models for 20 preselected genes were selected using patient-grouped nested cross-validation in 681 models and evaluated in a locked 171-model holdout. Historical target selection used all 852 models, making holdout performance conditional internal confirmation rather than an unbiased generalization estimate. After refitting on all 852 models, frozen models underwent exploratory evaluation in 94 Broad organoids and blinded validation in 148 Sanger organoids from 144 donors. Predictions were sealed before Sanger outcome access. Primary target-wise Spearman correlations, ranking organoids per gene, averaged 0.4094, 0.1518, and 0.1015 in holdout, Broad, and Sanger, respectively. Sanger association exceeded the within-lineage permutation null (<italic>p</italic> = 0.00040), but improvement over lineage-only prediction remained uncertain (difference, 0.0462; 95% confidence interval, −0.0065–0.0986). <italic>CDK6</italic>, <italic>MDM4</italic>, and <italic>CCNE1</italic> passed false discovery rate correction in Sanger. Retrospective within-organoid gene ranking modestly improved over lineage-only prediction in both cohorts; top-three overlap improved only in Sanger. Pancreatic results remained unvalidated projections. Findings support weak cross-domain rank transfer and limited within-organoid ranking within the selected panel, without establishing genome-wide transferability, causal explanations for attenuation, or prospective experimental or therapeutic utility.</p></abstract><custom-meta-group><custom-meta><meta-name>status</meta-name><meta-value>released</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>display-pdf</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>is-olf</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>is-manuscript</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>is-preprint</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>is-journal-matter</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>is-scanned</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>is-retracted</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta></custom-meta-group></article-meta><notes notes-type="article-notes"><sec id="historyarticle-meta1" sec-type="history" disp-level="2"><p>Received 2026 Sep 15; Revised 2026 Sep 30; Accepted 2026 Oct 5; Collection date 2026 Oct.</p></sec></notes></front><body><sec id="sec1-biology-15-01782" disp-level="1"><title>1. Introduction</title><p>Cancer comprises a heterogeneous group of diseases driven not only by genetic and epigenetic alterations but also by the reorganization of cellular signaling networks. This heterogeneity contributes to variable treatment responses among tumors with the same histological diagnosis and limits the effectiveness of target selection based solely on genomic alterations [<xref rid="B1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">1</xref>]. Gene dependency refers to a cancer cell’s requirement to express a particular gene to survive or proliferate. Identifying such dependencies and synthetic-lethal relationships offers a strategy for exposing cancer-specific vulnerabilities while comparatively sparing normal cells [<xref rid="B2-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">2</xref>].</p><p>Large-scale functional genomic studies now enable the systematic interrogation of genes required for fitness across cancer models with diverse molecular backgrounds. The Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap) links molecular profiles of cancer cell lines to functional-screening data, enabling the identification of common and context-specific dependencies [<xref rid="B3-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">3</xref>,<xref rid="B4-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">4</xref>]. Genome-scale loss-of-function screens using clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) and CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9), collectively termed CRISPR–Cas9, have made systematic gene inactivation feasible in human cells [<xref rid="B5-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">5</xref>,<xref rid="B6-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">6</xref>]. High-resolution libraries have improved discrimination between core-essential genes and context-specific vulnerabilities [<xref rid="B7-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">7</xref>], whereas copy-number-associated cutting toxicity has motivated correction methods such as CERES [<xref rid="B8-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">8</xref>]. Large-scale ribonucleic acid (RNA) interference screens have provided complementary maps of dependency and synthetic lethality [<xref rid="B9-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">9</xref>]. Although Broad and Sanger dependency datasets show broad concordance, gene-effect estimates can vary across screening libraries, experimental protocols, and computational processing [<xref rid="B10-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">10</xref>,<xref rid="B11-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">11</xref>]. Methods such as Chronos seek to improve dependency estimation by accounting for cell-population dynamics [<xref rid="B12-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">12</xref>]. Nevertheless, genome-scale CRISPR screening remains costly, technically demanding, and sample-intensive, limiting its routine application across newly derived cancer models.</p><p>The Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) has established a molecular foundation for modeling associations among mutation, copy number, gene expression, treatment response, and gene dependency [<xref rid="B13-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">13</xref>,<xref rid="B14-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">14</xref>]. Although proteomic profiling expands this information space, messenger RNA expression remains an accessible readout of cellular state, measurable consistently across many cohorts [<xref rid="B15-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">15</xref>]. This availability has motivated the computational prediction of dependencies in samples without direct functional screening. DeepDEP demonstrated that multi-omic profiles can predict cancer dependencies [<xref rid="B16-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">16</xref>], while transcriptome-based dependency maps developed for The Cancer Genome Atlas showed that Elastic Net models can prioritize putative tumor vulnerabilities [<xref rid="B17-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">17</xref>]. Other approaches have used synthetic data augmentation to address incomplete molecular profiles [<xref rid="B18-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">18</xref>]. However, expression-dependency associations can reflect tissue of origin and shared transcriptional programs [<xref rid="B19-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">19</xref>], and domain shifts between cell lines and tumors can compromise transferability [<xref rid="B20-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">20</xref>]. Thus, strong performance within cell-line collections should not be equated with generalizability across biological model systems. Elastic Net is well suited to high-dimensional data because it combines regularization, variable selection, and stability in the presence of correlated features [<xref rid="B21-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">21</xref>]. Yet model selection and performance estimation on the same observations can produce optimistic bias, necessitating nested cross-validation [<xref rid="B22-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">22</xref>]. Likewise, samples derived from the same patient or biological source must remain within a common data partition to prevent information leakage [<xref rid="B23-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">23</xref>].</p><p>Conventional two-dimensional (2D) cultures are scalable and well-suited to functional screening, but they incompletely recapitulate cell–cell interactions, tissue architecture, and tumor-specific transcriptional states. Patient-derived organoids are three-dimensional (3D) culture systems that retain selected structural, genetic, and functional features of their tissue of origin [<xref rid="B24-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">24</xref>,<xref rid="B25-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">25</xref>]. Colorectal organoid biobanks have shown that interpatient molecular diversity and drug-response phenotypes can be preserved ex vivo [<xref rid="B26-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">26</xref>]. Comparisons with clinical outcomes also support the potential of gastrointestinal cancer organoids to reflect sensitivity or resistance to selected therapies [<xref rid="B27-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">27</xref>,<xref rid="B28-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">28</xref>]. These advantages make organoids valuable preclinical models for testing whether dependencies learned in 2D remain biologically relevant in more tissue-like systems. However, their epithelial predominance, incomplete representation of immune and stromal compartments, and sensitivity to culture conditions constrain direct extrapolation to patient tumors [<xref rid="B29-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">29</xref>].</p><p>In pancreatic cancer, long-term organoid cultures have been established from both normal and neoplastic tissues [<xref rid="B30-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">30</xref>], and growth-factor requirements have been shown to change with disease progression [<xref rid="B31-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">31</xref>]. The pancreatic organoid cohort reported by Tiriac et al. integrated RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) profiles with treatment-response phenotypes, enabling the analysis of molecular and functional subtypes [<xref rid="B32-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">32</xref>]. Subsequent biobanks have further demonstrated the preservation of disease features and the feasibility of individualized drug screening [<xref rid="B33-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">33</xref>]. However, most such cohorts lack genome-scale measured CRISPR dependency outcomes. Consequently, applying an expression-based dependency model to RNA-seq data from these resources can provide biological projections or candidate hypotheses for functional testing, but cannot by itself establish measured gene dependency or therapeutic sensitivity.</p><p>Direct functional screening in organoids is technically challenging, yet genome-scale studies in intestinal organoids have identified genes associated with growth and treatment resistance [<xref rid="B34-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">34</xref>]. Pooled screens in human colon organoids have revealed tumor-suppressor and context-dependent selection effects [<xref rid="B35-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">35</xref>], and more recent work has identified dependencies involving WNT, mitogen-activated protein kinase, phosphoinositide 3-kinase, p53, and deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) mismatch-repair pathways [<xref rid="B36-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">36</xref>]. Large-scale CRISPR knockout, CRISPR interference, and CRISPR activation screens in gastric organoids have further demonstrated the feasibility of examining gene-drug interactions in 3D systems [<xref rid="B37-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">37</xref>]. Next-generation model collections show that dependency profiles may differ between 2D and 3D culture conditions [<xref rid="B38-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">38</xref>]. Cancer dependencies can also be mapped systematically across tumor organoid biobanks [<xref rid="B39-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">39</xref>]. Expanded patient-derived model resources can capture substantial tumor diversity [<xref rid="B40-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">40</xref>]. Together, these studies establish organoids as increasingly tractable functional genomics platforms while also underscoring that culture context can alter the biological relationships inferred from conventional cell lines.</p><p>Despite these advances, the extent to which transcriptome-dependency relationships learned in 2D cancer cell lines transfer to independent 3D organoid cohorts remains unresolved. A rigorous assessment requires model selection to be completed without access to 3D outcomes, predictions to be locked before outcome evaluation, and performance to be tested across independently generated CRISPR datasets. Here, we developed target-specific, expression-based Elastic Net models for a fixed panel of 20 genes using 852 pan-cancer 2D models. Candidate molecular representations were compared using patient-grouped nested cross-validation. The selected model was evaluated once in a locked 2D holdout for internal confirmation conditional on historical target selection. Without outcome-guided retraining, the frozen model was then examined exploratorily in Broad organoids and subjected to blinded independent external validation in a non-overlapping Sanger organoid cohort. Target-level findings from the two 3D cohorts were integrated in a retrospective transportability synthesis, and the locked models were subsequently projected onto an independent pancreatic organoid RNA-seq cohort lacking measured CRISPR outcomes. The primary hypothesis concerned ranking organoids by measured dependency for each gene, not ranking genes within an individual organoid. We hypothesized that this between-organoid signal would remain detectable but attenuated in 3D systems. A separate retrospective analysis evaluated gene ranking within individual organoids using the same frozen predictions. This secondary analysis addressed a different prediction task and did not replace the original primary evaluation.</p></sec><sec id="sec2-biology-15-01782" disp-level="1"><title>2. Materials and Methods</title><sec id="sec2dot1-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>2.1. Study Design and Data Sources</title><p>This retrospective, multi-cohort computational study evaluated whether transcriptome-based gene-dependency rankings learned in 2D cancer models could be transferred to independent 3D organoid systems. The study used publicly available or openly released molecular, transcriptomic, and functional-genomics resources; it collected no new biospecimens and performed no new CRISPR screens. The primary workflow comprised five analytically distinct layers: (i) patient-grouped 2D model development and locking; (ii) exploratory transfer assessment in Broad organoids; (iii) outcome-blinded independent external validation in Sanger organoids; (iv) retrospective synthesis of the Broad and Sanger target-level results; and (v) secondary transcriptomic projection in a pancreatic organoid cohort without measured CRISPR dependency outcomes. The primary study design, data sources, and evidence hierarchy are shown in <xref rid="biology-15-01782-f001" ref-type="fig">Figure 1</xref>. A separate retrospective analysis of gene ranking within organoids was defined after the external outcomes were available (<xref rid="sec2dot10dot1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.10.1</xref>; <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Tables S17–S19</xref>).</p><fig id="biology-15-01782-f001" position="float"><?disp-level 3?><label>Figure 1</label><caption><p>Study design, data sources, and evidence hierarchy. Target-specific Elastic Net models were developed from transcriptomic profiles and CRISPR Gene Effect values in 852 two-dimensional cancer models obtained from DepMap Public 26Q1 and the CCLE. Candidate representations were compared in 681 development models, and the selected expression-only representation was evaluated once on a locked 171-model internal holdout set; the final models were then refitted on all 852 models, keeping the targets, target-specific features, hyperparameters, and primary metric fixed. Historical target selection included the holdout models, so this evaluation provides internal confirmation conditional on the selected panel. Without retraining, these models were applied to 94 Broad NextGen organoids for exploratory evaluation and to 148 Sanger organoids representing 144 donors for blinded independent external validation. Sanger predictions were sealed using the 256-bit Secure Hash Algorithm before access to CRISPR outcomes. Broad and Sanger target-level results were subsequently combined in a retrospective transportability synthesis. The Tiriac pancreatic RNA-sequencing cohort comprised 55 samples and was used only for secondary projection because measured genome-scale CRISPR dependency outcomes were unavailable. The dashed border identifies this non-validation application cohort. The figure depicts the primary workflow; the model specification and prespecified primary metric remained unchanged. The separate retrospective within-organoid ranking analysis is described in <xref rid="sec2dot10dot1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.10.1</xref> and <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Tables S17–S19</xref> and was not a new blinded validation. Colored boxes distinguish the five labeled stages, and arrows indicate their order in the workflow. CCLE, Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia; CRISPR, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats; DepMap, Cancer Dependency Map; RNA, ribonucleic acid; SHA-256, 256-bit Secure Hash Algorithm.</p></caption><alternatives><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="image" xlink:href="biology-15-01782-g001.webp"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/78de/13664187/76c7e31e9f46/biology-15-01782-g001.webp?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?><?image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?original-height 1853?><?original-width 1467?><?scaled-height 1853?><?scaled-width 1467?></graphic><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="thumb" xlink:href="biology-15-01782-g001.gif"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/78de/13664187/c1ccb192f556/biology-15-01782-g001.gif?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?></graphic></alternatives></fig><p>As shown in <xref rid="biology-15-01782-f001" ref-type="fig">Figure 1</xref>, the first layer comprised 2D model development and locking using DepMap Public 26Q1 and CCLE molecular data [<xref rid="B3-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">3</xref>,<xref rid="B4-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">4</xref>,<xref rid="B13-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">13</xref>,<xref rid="B14-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">14</xref>]. The analysis-ready population included 852 pan-cancer models with continuous CRISPR Gene Effect values for a fixed 20-gene target panel. Models were partitioned by PatientID, with ModelID used as a fallback only when PatientID was unavailable. This yielded 681 development models from 658 patient groups and 171 locked internal-holdout models from 165 patient groups. No PatientID was shared between partitions. Candidate molecular representations were compared exclusively within the development partition using patient-grouped, lineage-stratified 5 × 5 nested cross-validation. Before the locked-holdout outcomes were evaluated, the selected representation, target panel, target-specific feature identities, hyperparameters, primary metric, and prediction files were frozen. After the one-time holdout evaluation, the selected expression-only Elastic Net specification was refitted on all 852 models for downstream deployment. Only imputation, scaling, and coefficient parameters were re-estimated. The targets, features, hyperparameters, and primary metric remained fixed.</p><p>The second layer used 94 organoids from the Broad NextGen cancer model resource, with matched gene expression and CRISPR Gene Effect values for all 20 targets [<xref rid="B38-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">38</xref>]. The all-852 deployment model was applied without Broad-specific retraining, recalibration, feature substitution, or coefficient adaptation. Because PatientID was unavailable in the original Broad evaluation records, the organoid model was initially the analysis and resampling unit. Subsequently recovered partial donor information was examined retrospectively in <xref rid="sec2dot10dot3-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.10.3</xref>. Although the audited current run preserved a prediction-before-outcome sequence, Broad-94 had been accessible during earlier methodological work and was therefore classified as a retrospective exploratory transfer cohort rather than a pristine independent validation set.</p><p>The third layer used the Sanger tumor-derived organoid dependency map [<xref rid="B39-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">39</xref>]. Following cross-resource identity auditing and conservative exclusion of Broad-linked and same-donor records, the final cohort contained 148 organoids from 144 donors. The fixed 20-target prediction matrix, cohort registry, protocol, and model and feature manifests were written and cryptographically sealed using the 256-bit Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA-256) before Sanger CRISPR outcomes were accessed. Sanger-148 was therefore treated as a one-time, outcome-blinded independent external-validation cohort, with donor structure retained in uncertainty estimation and sensitivity analyses.</p><p>In the fourth layer, the Broad-94 and Sanger-148 target-level rank correlations were combined only after the two cohorts had been evaluated separately [<xref rid="B38-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">38</xref>,<xref rid="B39-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">39</xref>]. The retrospective transportability synthesis assessed directional concordance, pooled target-level associations, and between-cohort heterogeneity. It was not treated as a third external validation and did not alter any component of the frozen model. Because Broad/DepMap Chronos Gene Effect and Sanger corrected CRISPR log fold change (LFC) values are assay-specific scales, the synthesis focused on rank transfer rather than absolute numerical equivalence.</p><p>The fifth layer applied the same frozen models to 55 RNA-seq samples from the Tiriac pancreatic organoid cohort, accessed through the Genomic Data Commons (GDC) ORGANOID-PANCREATIC project [<xref rid="B32-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">32</xref>]. The resource comprised 44 tumor samples from 38 independent tumor cases and 11 normal samples from 11 independent normal cases. Because measured genome-scale CRISPR dependency outcomes were unavailable, this layer was restricted to secondary transcriptomic projection and expression-domain diagnostics and was not used to estimate predictive accuracy or therapeutic sensitivity. Across all layers, no 3D observation contributed to 2D candidate selection, feature learning, hyperparameter tuning, or deployment coefficient estimation. After access to 3D data, no retraining, recalibration, target or feature reselection, hyperparameter retuning, or replacement of the prespecified primary metric was permitted. Omics Data Preprocessing and Candidate Input Representations</title><p>The candidate omics blocks were derived from processed molecular data in DepMap Public 26Q1 and aligned to the 852 models defined in <xref rid="sec2dot2-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.2</xref> [<xref rid="B3-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">3</xref>,<xref rid="B13-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">13</xref>,<xref rid="B14-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">14</xref>]. We used a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the 20 paired differences to assess the incremental contribution of expression beyond lineage. A retrospective evidence classification was used for reporting only. Tier A required a positive correlation in both cohorts, a meta-analytic FDR q < 0.05, and target-level FDR q < 0.05 in at least one individual cohort. Tier B indicated positive correlations in both cohorts without fulfillment of all Tier A criteria. Tier C indicated a non-positive correlation in at least one cohort. As specified in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S7</xref>, the evidence tiers did not alter the locked panel or any model component, and no retraining, target or feature reselection, hyperparameter tuning, metric switching, or direction-based target removal was permitted during the synthesis.</p></sec><sec id="sec2dot9-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>2.9. Secondary Transcriptomic Projection in the Tiriac Pancreatic Organoid Cohort</title><p>After completion of 2D model development, Broad-94 exploration, Sanger-148 blinded validation, and the retrospective cross-cohort synthesis, the frozen expression-only deployment models were applied to the Tiriac/ORGANOID-PANCREATIC cohort as a secondary biological projection [<xref rid="B32-biology-15-01782" ref-type="bibr">32</xref>]. Because measured genome-scale CRISPR dependency outcomes were unavailable, this analysis was prespecified as an application to an independent pancreatic transcriptome rather than external validation; predictive accuracy and CRISPR performance were not estimated. Fifty-five publicly available RNA-seq Spliced Transcripts Alignment to a Reference (STAR) count files from the GDC project were obtained from the official public Amazon Simple Storage Service mirror. The cohort comprised 44 tumor samples representing 38 independent tumor cases and 11 samples from 11 independent normal cases; group membership was defined from the source TissueType metadata. Cohort preparation and projection procedures are summarized in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S8</xref>.</p><p>The tpm_unstranded field in the STAR output was used as the abundance measure. Rows mapping to the same gene symbol were summed at the TPM level before log2(TPM + 1) transformation. The resulting sample-by-feature matrix was aligned to the locked expression features of the 20 target-specific Elastic Net deployment bundles finalized in all 852 2D models. The target panel, target-specific feature identities, stored imputation and standardization objects, hyperparameters, coefficients, and projection definitions were applied without modification. No Tiriac sample contributed to model fitting, feature selection, recalibration, retuning, or endpoint definition.</p><p>Of the 3845 unique locked features used across the 20 models, 3806 were observed in the Tiriac data. Target-specific coverage ranged from 292 to 300 of 300 selected features (97.33–100%), and every target met the prespecified 80% coverage threshold. Features absent from the Tiriac matrix were represented as not-a-number (NaN) values, filled with the medians stored in the frozen all-852 deployment models before the stored standardization, and then coefficients were applied. This preserved the training preprocessing rule without estimating replacement values from Tiriac. An independent computational replay reproduced the archived predictions exactly using training-median imputation (<xref rid="sec2dot10dot2-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.10.2</xref>). This procedure produced a 55-sample × 20-target projection matrix. Source file identifiers, file sizes, source-provided integrity values, local SHA-256 digests, model and feature manifests, and prediction records were retained for provenance.</p><p>When multiple tumor organoid samples originated from the same GDC case, the 20 sample-level projections were averaged within the case, and the patient/case was used as the inferential unit. For each target, median case-level projections were calculated for 38 tumor cases and 11 normal cases, together with the tumor-minus-normal median difference. Uncertainty in this difference was estimated using 5000 case-level bootstrap resamples within the tumor and normal groups, with 95% percentile intervals. Tumor and normal projection distributions were compared using two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests, and the 20 <italic>p</italic>-values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR procedure. Cliff’s delta was reported as an effect-size measure; under the prespecified orientation, a positive value indicated a more negative, and therefore stronger, projected dependency distribution in tumors. These analyses compared frozen model outputs rather than measured dependencies or model errors.</p><p>The 20-target median projection vector for Tiriac tumor cases was compared separately with the corresponding median prediction vectors for Broad-94 and Sanger-148. This comparison assessed whether the projected pancreatic target hierarchy was consistent across organoid applications. Concordance was quantified using two-sided Spearman correlations across the 20 targets. Because all compared values were predictions from the same locked model family and Tiriac lacked measured CRISPR outcomes, these correlations were interpreted as secondary evidence of target-ranking consistency rather than independent evidence of predictive accuracy.</p><p>Expression-domain shift was evaluated across the 3790 locked expression features that are jointly available in Tiriac, Broad-94, and Sanger-148. Multivariable separation among cohorts was visualized by principal component analysis (PCA). For Tiriac versus Broad-94 and Tiriac versus Sanger-148, a standardized mean difference (SMD) was calculated for each common feature, and shift magnitude was summarized using the median absolute SMD and the proportions of features with |SMD| > 1 and |SMD| > 2. The PCA and SMD diagnostics were descriptive and were not used to recalibrate the models, delete features, remove targets, or revise projections. <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S8</xref> defines the corresponding claim boundary: Tiriac results were described as projections or prioritizations and not as validated dependencies, confirmed dependencies, or therapeutic sensitivity.</p></sec><sec id="sec2dot10-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>2.10. Statistical Analysis</title><p>Statistical analyses preserved the prespecified role and strongest available biological independence unit of each study layer. In the development, locked 2D holdout, Broad-94, and Sanger-148 analyses, the primary rank-based measure was the Spearman correlation between predicted and observed outcomes for each target and the arithmetic mean of the 20 target correlations (macro target-wise Spearman correlation). MAE, RMSE, R<sup>2</sup>, calibration intercept, and calibration slope were secondary diagnostics in the development, locked-holdout, and Broad analyses and did not reopen model selection. Because Sanger-corrected LFC and DepMap/Broad Chronos Gene Effect values were not treated as numerically equivalent, the Sanger validation and cross-cohort synthesis were based on rank correlation rather than absolute-scale error. Target-wise correlation operates across organoids for each gene; within-organoid correlation instead operates across the 20 genes for each organoid. Averaging target-wise correlations does not test within-organoid gene ranking. The original analysis hierarchy, inferential units, resampling procedures, and multiplicity rules are summarized in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S9</xref>; the retrospective within-organoid endpoints are defined in <xref rid="sec2dot10dot1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.10.1</xref> and <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Tables S17–S19</xref>.</p><p>Resampling units followed the available biological grouping. Development and locked 2D holdout uncertainty used 2000 PatientID-cluster bootstrap replicates, retaining all models from a sampled patient group together. Broad-94 used 5000 model-level bootstrap replicates within OncotreeLineage strata because PatientID was unavailable in the original evaluation records; the later partial-donor sensitivities are reported separately in <xref rid="sec2dot10dot3-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Section 2.10.3</xref>. Sanger-148 used 5000 donor-cluster bootstrap replicates, retaining all organoids from a sampled donor together. Tiriac tumor-normal comparisons used 5000 case-level bootstrap replicates within the 38-tumor and 11-normal groups. Unless otherwise specified, 95% percentile CIs were defined by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. Paired model comparisons used common resampling indices. The standard error used in the development one-standard-error rule was derived from the 2000-replicate PatientID-cluster bootstrap distribution of OOF predictions.</p><p>For permutation analyses, predictions remained fixed and complete 20-target observed-outcome vectors were moved without disrupting the prespecified biological grouping. The locked 2D sensitivity analysis used 2000 one-sided permutations of patient-aggregated outcome vectors within OncotreeLineage strata. Broad-94 used 5000 one-sided permutations of ModelID-level outcome vectors within lineage. Sanger-148 used 5000 two-sided permutations after donor averaging, with donor-level outcome vectors moved within tumor-type/lineage strata and the absolute macro correlation used as the test statistic. Empirical <italic>p</italic>-values used the standard plus-one numerator and denominator correction. Broad and Sanger target-specific permutation <italic>p</italic>-values were adjusted separately within their 20-target families using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR procedure.</p><p>In the retrospective cross-cohort synthesis, common-positive direction was assessed with a one-sided exact binomial benchmark (<italic>n</italic> = 20; null probability = 0.50), interpreted descriptively because targets were correlated and the synthesis was retrospective. Target-specific correlations were pooled on the Fisher-z scale using inverse-variance fixed-effect weights derived from cohort-specific bootstrap uncertainty, and the 20 two-sided meta-analytic <italic>p</italic>-values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Random-effects estimates and I<sup>2</sup> were descriptive because only two cohorts were available. Target-panel sensitivity used 20,000 target-bootstrap resamples, while cross-target dependence was assessed using 50,000 one-sided simultaneous block permutations at the Broad ModelID and Sanger donor-mean levels. Expression-only-minus-lineage target differences were evaluated separately in Broad and Sanger using one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. None of these retrospective analyses was interpreted as a new validation cohort.</p><p>In the Tiriac layer, two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests compared patient-level tumor and normal projections for each target. Benjamini–Hochberg FDR adjustment was applied across 20 tests. Cliff’s delta described effect direction. Concordance between the Tiriac tumor target-median vector and the Broad and Sanger target-median prediction vectors was evaluated using two-sided Spearman correlations across 20 targets. We used PCA and SMD measures only as descriptive domain-shift diagnostics, and they did not inform the confirmatory decision.</p><p>A retrospective coverage-threshold sensitivity analysis compared the prespecified 80% rule with stricter 90% and 95% requirements using the archived target-specific present-feature counts. The number of eligible models among the fixed 20 targets was recorded for each external cohort. Only the eligibility requirement was varied; no features were removed, no models were refitted, and no missing-feature handling was changed (<xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S16</xref>).</p><p>Tests were two-sided unless explicitly prespecified as one-sided. Within each stated 20-target family, FDR q < 0.05 defined the multiplicity-adjusted target-level significance; exact <italic>p</italic>-values, effect sizes, and CIs were reported together where applicable. Exploratory and post hoc analyses retained those labels even when a statistical threshold was crossed, and no analysis result changed the target panel, feature identities, hyperparameters, primary metrics, or previously generated predictions. Analyses were implemented in Python 3.12.13 using NumPy 2.3.5, pandas 2.2.3, SciPy 1.17.0, scikit-learn 1.8.0, and joblib 1.5.3. Random seeds, environment files, protocols, SHA-256 manifests, and integrity checks were preserved in the archived reproducibility package.</p><sec id="sec2dot10dot1-biology-15-01782" disp-level="3"><title>2.10.1. Retrospective Evaluation of Gene Ranking Within Organoids</title><p>A retrospective secondary analysis evaluated whether the frozen expression-only predictions ranked the 20 genes within individual organoids in agreement with measured CRISPR outcomes. This secondary analysis was defined after the external outcomes were available and was not a new blinded validation. It retained all 20 targets and all 94 Broad and 148 Sanger organoids; Tiriac was excluded because measured dependency outcomes were unavailable. No predictions, models, features, hyperparameters, or targets were changed, and the original target-wise primary analysis was retained.</p><p>For each organoid, we calculated Spearman correlation across its 20 predicted and 20 observed scores, using average ranks for ties, and summarized the correlations by their arithmetic mean. Lower scores denoted stronger measured or predicted dependency. The main comparator assigned every organoid the same per-gene mean of the observed outcomes across all 852 2D training models, with each training model weighted equally. This fixed ranking tested whether expression predictions improved on gene-level average dependency. We also reused the archived lineage-only predictions: the ridge reference in Broad and patient-weighted 2D lineage means in Sanger. No external outcomes were used to fit either comparator (<xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S17</xref>).</p><p>To examine a short candidate list, we calculated the overlap between the three lowest predicted scores and the three lowest measured scores, divided by three, within each organoid. The cohort mean was expressed as a percentage. Ties at the selection boundary were to be resolved by the fixed target identifiers; none occurred. Expression-minus-comparator differences were calculated within the same organoids for both the full-ranking correlation and top-three overlap (<xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S18</xref>). These endpoints assess agreement with measured CRISPR score ordering within the selected panel, not cancer selectivity, cross-gene calibration, drug response, or clinical benefit.</p><p>We estimated 95% percentile CIs using 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples: organoid models sampled within observed lineage strata for Broad, and donor clusters sampled with all their organoids retained together for Sanger. The Sanger main estimate remained organoid-weighted. A donor-level sensitivity analysis first averaged the predicted and observed 20-gene vectors within each of 144 donors, then recalculated both endpoints with equal donor weights and a 10,000-replicate donor bootstrap (<xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S19</xref>). Seeds were 20260928, 20260929, and 20260930 for Broad, Sanger, and donor-mean sensitivity, respectively. All correlations were defined. Intervals were conditional on the frozen models and fixed panel; they did not include model-training or gene-panel selection uncertainty. The secondary comparisons were not adjusted for multiplicity and were interpreted as exploratory.</p></sec><sec id="sec2dot10dot2-biology-15-01782" disp-level="3"><title>2.10.2. Retrospective Sensitivity to Missing-Feature Imputation in Tiriac</title><p>A retrospective sensitivity analysis evaluated the effects of alternative missing-feature replacement values on Tiriac projections. This descriptive analysis was not prespecified. The archived code represented absent inputs as NaN and applied the frozen training-median imputer, followed by the stored scaler and Elastic Net estimator. This pipeline reproduced all 1100 archived Tiriac predictions exactly. The reference predictions were generated with training medians and were retained for comparison with the alternative imputation methods. The 39 absent unique features corresponded to 0–8 missing predictors per target, with the same missing-feature pattern across all 55 samples.</p><p>Using the same frozen models, we compared training-median imputation with two alternatives: zero on the log2(TPM + 1) scale before standardization, and the stored training-reference mean for each feature. These means were estimated after median imputation in the 852-model training data and correspond to zero standardized input, up to floating-point rounding. Only absent features were replaced; observed expression values, including measured zeros, were retained. We summarized absolute projection changes, Spearman correlation across the 20 genes within each profile, and top-three set overlap relative to the median-imputed reference. We evaluated sample-level results and case-averaged profiles, including 38 tumor and 11 normal cases. We also repeated the original tumor–normal comparisons using the same 5000 bootstrap resamples (seed 20260830), Mann–Whitney tests, and 20-target FDR adjustment. These are descriptive checks of projection stability, not prediction accuracy. Because the models are linear and the missing-feature pattern is shared, constant replacement values create a common offset per target; preservation of within-target sample ranks and tumor–normal differences is therefore expected algebraically (<xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Tables S20 and S21</xref>).</p></sec><sec id="sec2dot10dot3-biology-15-01782" disp-level="3"><title>2.10.3. Retrospective Broad Donor Audit and Sensitivity Analyses</title><p>A retrospective metadata audit linked 16 of the 94 models to 15 PatientID values in the supplied DepMap Model.csv and nine additional models to nine source-specific donor identifiers in the archived Sanger exclusion registry. Thus, donor information was available for 25 models, forming 24 source-specific groups, while 69 models remained unresolved. ACH-002883 and ACH-002884 shared PatientID PT-N65Hvq. The DepMap and Sanger donor namespaces could not be fully reconciled, so the 24 groups do not establish 24 independently verified biological donors. No donor identity was inferred from lineage or model-name similarity (<xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S22</xref>).</p><p>Retrospective sensitivity analyses used the unchanged predictions, outcomes, and 20-gene panel. Each member of the known same-donor pair was omitted in turn. A conditional full-cohort bootstrap grouped the known pair and treated unresolved models as singleton units, yielding 93 resampling groups; this assumption does not establish independence of the 69 unresolved models. In the donor-documented subset, model-level and donor-cluster bootstraps were compared on the same 25 models, and a separate analysis averaged prediction, outcome, and lineage-reference vectors within the 24 source-specific donor groups before evaluation. All analyses used 5000 paired bootstrap replicates within the observed OncotreeLineage strata (seed 20260929), retaining every model from each sampled group. Percentile 95% intervals were calculated at 2.5% and 97.5%. Target-wise correlations were reranked within each resample and averaged across all 20 targets; an undefined target correlation contributed zero, following the archived convention. Organoid weighting was retained except in the donor-mean analysis. Full-cohort and known-subset model-level replays with the same seed provide matched references; they do not replace the original CIs. <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Tables S23 and S24</xref> report the primary target-wise and secondary within-organoid endpoints. These post hoc intervals were not adjusted for multiple sensitivity comparisons, and no new confirmatory permutation or FDR claim was made.</p></sec></sec><sec id="sec2dot11-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>2.11. All 20 target-specific feature sets had 100% coverage. Eighteen target estimates were positive, but no target passed Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction at q < 0.05. Broad-94 remained exploratory and was not treated as independent external validation. In (<bold>b</bold>), filled blue circles denote positive correlations, whereas open circles denote non-positive correlations; the solid black line marks zero correlation. Blue solid lines in (<bold>c</bold>,<bold>d</bold>) mark the observed macro correlation. Blue histogram bars in (<bold>c</bold>) show bootstrap replicates, and gray histogram bars in (<bold>d</bold>) show permutation-null replicates. 2D, two-dimensional; BH, Benjamini–Hochberg; CI, confidence interval; FDR, false discovery rate; OOF, out-of-fold.</p></caption><alternatives><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="image" xlink:href="biology-15-01782-g004.webp"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/78de/13664187/45c6b8b784d7/biology-15-01782-g004.webp?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?><?image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?original-height 1722?><?original-width 1600?><?scaled-height 1722?><?scaled-width 1600?></graphic><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="thumb" xlink:href="biology-15-01782-g004.gif"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/78de/13664187/18962c46d2d5/biology-15-01782-g004.gif?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?></graphic></alternatives></fig><p>As shown in <xref rid="biology-15-01782-f004" ref-type="fig">Figure 4</xref>a,c,d, the macro target-wise Spearman correlation in Broad-94 was 0.1518 (95% lineage-stratified bootstrap CI, 0.1019–0.2006). Eighteen of 20 target correlations were positive, and the median target correlation was 0.1628. The Broad-94 macro correlation was 0.2576 lower than the locked 2D holdout value. In the within-lineage permutation analysis, an association at least as large as the observed value occurred rarely (one-sided <italic>p</italic> = 0.00080), supporting partial but attenuated transfer of rank information.</p><p>The lineage-adjusted macro Spearman correlation was 0.1080, whereas the lineage-only reference yielded 0.0951. The paired expression-only-minus-lineage-only difference was +0.0567 (95% CI, 0.0040–0.1106). Thus, lineage composition did not fully explain the exploratory association, although it accounted for part of the observed signal.</p><p>At the target level, the highest correlations were observed for <italic>ERBB3</italic> (ρ = 0.3489), <italic>CCNE1</italic> (ρ = 0.3456), <italic>CTNNB1</italic> (ρ = 0.3009), <italic>E2F3</italic> (ρ = 0.2679), and <italic>YAP1</italic> (ρ = 0.2614) (<xref rid="biology-15-01782-f004" ref-type="fig">Figure 4</xref>b; <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S12</xref>). <italic>MAPK1</italic> (ρ = −0.0307) and <italic>STK11</italic> (ρ = −0.1010) were the only targets with negative correlations. After adjustment of the 20 target-level permutation <italic>p</italic> values, no target met the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR threshold of <italic>q</italic> < 0.05; the lowest adjusted value was <italic>q</italic> = 0.0640 for <italic>CCNE1</italic>. Accordingly, Broad-94 was interpreted at the fixed-panel level rather than as confirmatory evidence for individual targets.</p><p>Among lineage groups containing at least seven models, macro correlations ranged from −0.0099 to 0.2786. Leave-one-lineage-out estimates ranged from 0.1202 to 0.1832, and the pooled association remained positive after every lineage exclusion. The original estimates used model-level resampling. The subsequent donor audit and sensitivity analyses below address the identified shared donor, while retaining uncertainty about unresolved donor relationships.</p><p>The donor audit identified one confirmed same-donor pair among 25 models with donor information; 69 models remained unresolved (<xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S22</xref>). Omitting ACH-002883 or ACH-002884 gave macro target-wise correlations of 0.1516 and 0.1539, respectively, compared with the original 0.1518. Under the conditional full-cohort bootstrap, the expression-only estimate was 0.1518 (0.1009 to 0.2007) and its paired difference from lineage-only prediction was 0.0567 (0.0027 to 0.1081) (estimate and 95% CI; <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S23</xref>). These findings quantify sensitivity to the identified pair, conditional on treating the unresolved models as separate units.</p><p>In the 25-model donor-documented subset, the expression-only macro correlation was 0.0741 (−0.0154 to 0.1618), with an expression-minus-lineage difference of −0.0571 (−0.1502 to 0.0305) under source-specific donor-cluster resampling. Both intervals included zero, so this subset did not establish superiority over lineage. Averaging the vectors within the 24 source-specific donor groups gave 0.0727 (−0.0195 to 0.1629) for expression-only prediction. This subset is not a representative replacement for Broad-94; changes relative to the full cohort can reflect sample and lineage composition as well as grouping. Paired within-subset model-versus-cluster intervals and secondary ranking sensitivities are provided in <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Tables S23 and S24</xref>. Incomplete donor ascertainment prevents these analyses from verifying full-cohort independence or providing a fully donor-adjusted effective sample size.</p></sec><sec id="sec3dot4-biology-15-01782" disp-level="2"><title>3.4. Blinded Independent External Validation in Sanger-148 Organoids</title><p>The outcome-blinded Sanger eligibility pool comprised 162 organoids from 157 donors with both RNA-seq profiles and quality-controlled CRISPR screening records. After excluding 13 Broad-linked organoids and one additional organoid from the same donor as a Broad-linked model, the independent validation cohort contained 148 organoids from 144 unique donors. Of the 3845 unique locked expression features used across the 20 target models, 3790 were measured in the Sanger matrix; target-specific coverage ranged from 291 to 300 of 300 features (97.0–100%). The 148 × 20 blind prediction matrix and the associated manifests were SHA-256 sealed before CRISPR LFC outcomes were accessed, and all 11 prespecified pre-outcome seal checks passed. Panel-wide validation, target-level results, and robustness analyses are summarized in <xref rid="biology-15-01782-f005" ref-type="fig">Figure 5</xref> and <xref rid="app1-biology-15-01782" ref-type="sec">Table S13</xref>.</p><fig id="biology-15-01782-f005" position="float"><?disp-level 3?><label>Figure 5</label><caption><p>Blinded independent external validation in Sanger-148 organoids.
